summary: Describes the IETF's wishes for the rights that the IETF Trust should grant on IETF contributions, including Internet-Drafts and RFCs. Contributors grant rights to the IETF, and the Trustees manage them, including licenses to copy and implement, following direction from the IETF.

eli5.summary: People who write for the IETF give it permission to share their work. This tells the people holding that permission how widely to let others use it.

questions: what rights does the ietf trust grant
can i copy code from an rfc
subtitle: What the IETF wants the IETF Trust to let people do with RFCs and other IETF documents.

tldr.problem: Contributors give rights to the IETF, and the IETF Trust passes some of them on to the public. The Trustees need to know what the IETF wants those outbound rights to be.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states the IETF's wishes: anyone may copy and translate RFCs in full, quote excerpts with attribution, and extract, modify and use code components. It leaves the exact legal wording to the Trustees.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5377 only to remove references to the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC). The Trustees keep the authority to write the actual license text.

today: RFC 8721 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 5377 solely to remove references to the IAOC, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It expresses the IETF's wishes and leaves the actual license wording to the Trustees of the IETF Trust.

sections.title: Who Decides What Rights Are Granted
sections.content:
IETF intellectual property rights are vested in the IETF Trust, which is run by a board of trustees. Contributors grant rights to the IETF under the rules in RFC 5378, and the Trustees are responsible for defining the rights to copy that the IETF passes on to people who want to use the material.

The Trust has said it will respect the wishes of the IETF about those rights, so it is the IETF's job to state them. This document is that statement, until it is superseded. It uses the terminology of RFC 5378.
sections.eli5: A club keeps a shared toy box for everyone. The club members tell the box keeper how freely other kids may borrow the toys.

sections.title: Why Rights Are Granted
sections.content:
The IETF's mission is to produce documents that make the Internet work better. For standards that describe protocols, the main value is that implementors can build interoperable solutions, so the IETF wants accurate, interoperable implementations. Rights to copy are granted to encourage that. The same reasoning applies to Internet-Drafts, because early implementations are built from them, and to non-standard documents such as BCPs and Informational RFCs. The RFC recommends one common approach for all IETF documents.

Earlier documents put specific legal text inside the RFC. That proved problematic: fixing a legal problem meant revising the RFC, which delays urgent fixes. So this document describes the IETF's goals but gives no legal wording. Choosing and updating the wording is left to the Trustees.
sections.eli5: The goal is that anyone building something from the rulebook can read it and copy the parts they need. The grown-ups describe the goal and let the lawyers pick the exact words.

sections.title: Powers and Limits of the Trustees
sections.content:
The legal authority to grant users rights to copy RFCs and other IETF Contributions rests with the Trustees. This document gives guidance based on rough consensus of the IETF. The Trustees decide the exact text insertions or other mechanisms, if any, and changes to document policies take effect as the Trustees determine. The starting point is the license text created under RFC 5377.

The document does not say what rights the Trust receives from contributors; that is left to RFC 5378. It also notes that the Trust cannot grant rights it has not received, and rights for pre-existing documents cannot be expanded unless the rights holders agree. Where possible and without a massive effort, similar rights to those described would be desirable for older RFCs.
sections.eli5: The box keeper can only lend out what was put in the box. If someone kept a toy's rights, the keeper cannot lend it more freely than the owner allowed.

sections.title: Recommended Grants of Right to Copy
sections.content:
The recommendations are about outbound rights, meaning what the Trust passes on to others. They are separate from the rights the IETF itself needs to do its job.

  • Reproduction (4.1): anyone may make full copies and translations of RFCs. Copying in full spreads the material without losing context or meaning.
  • Quoting (4.2): unmodified excerpts of any length and in any context may be quoted, and quotations may be translated. They should be attributed to the IETF and the Contribution they come from.
  • Code (4.3): code components such as ABNF, XML Schemas, MIBs, ASN.1 and programming code can be extracted, modified and used by anyone in any way desired. The Trust should avoid adding software license obligations, and derived works outside the IETF may carry their own. This cannot apply to Contributions explicitly marked as not permitting derivative works.
  • Text (4.4): there is no consensus to permit using RFC text where the right to modify it is required. Authors may grant such rights independently.

For code, the Trustees are asked to keep an easily accessible list of RFC components considered to be code and to define a textual marking that identifies code in a Contribution.
sections.eli5: You may copy the whole book, quote a page if you say where it came from, and borrow and change the recipe parts for your own kitchen. Rewriting the story text itself is not covered.

sections.title: Additional Licenses
sections.content:
Sometimes the material in a Contribution is also available under other license terms. The IETF wants to be able to include such content and prefers that the Contribution indicate other licenses exist. However, the IETF does not want Contributions to carry additional licenses, and any extra text or referenced license must not restrict the rights the IETF intends to grant to others.

Authors keep all rights in their Contributions and may grant any rights separately. A reader who wants to use such grants must consult external sources or contact the author.
sections.eli5: An author can offer extra permissions on their own. They must not take back the permissions the club already gave everyone.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document assigns no values, creates no registries and gives IANA no action. It anticipates one list, of the kinds of code sections, created and maintained by the Trustees. They decide whether to create it and whether to involve IANA.

It introduces no new security considerations. It is a process document about IETF rights being granted to others, and it does not address attacks on the integrity or effectiveness of IETF processes.
sections.eli5: This is a paperwork rule, so it does not create new locks to pick or new doors to guard.
